## What population would you claim this applies to? {#population-question .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Choose a claim and defend its limits · 3 minutes</p>
<div class="claim-options">
<div class="claim-option"><b>A</b><span>Further L1 preparations under these conditions</span></div>
<div class="claim-option"><b>B</b><span>Other cell lines and donors</span></div>
<div class="claim-option"><b>C</b><span>Patients receiving the compound</span></div>
</div>
<p class="takeaway fragment">What would you need to know before choosing A?</p>

::: notes
**Time: 00:48–00:56 (8 minutes).**

**Say:** Three minutes in pairs, three minutes hearing two arguments, two minutes to debrief. A is the intended narrow target, not a guaranteed extrapolation. Ask whether the six preparations and three days cover the conditions they mean by “these conditions,” and whether selection, QC or unrecorded batches matter. Fold the previous separate scope-of-replication slide into this debrief: repeated preparations of L1 cover preparation variation; other cell lines or donors require additional biological sampling, and a claim across laboratories needs evidence relevant to laboratories. More assay readings of these lysates cannot supply those missing systems. B requires sampling additional biological systems. C requires a much broader chain of evidence; do not turn this into a clinical-trial lecture.

**Conceptual point:** A claim's population must match what was sampled and the assumptions used to extend beyond it. More distant generalizations require additional evidence.

**Likely misconception:** A is automatically justified once N is reported, or any in-vitro result directly represents patients.

**Optional follow-up:** What difference between your sampled preparations and future preparations worries you most?

**Sources:** R pp. 27–33, 45–47; A pp. 63, 71; D pp. 18–20. This is the approved eight-minute claim/population exercise. Do not introduce numerical inference to decide representativity.
:::

## Our sample and its population {#sample-population}

<div class="scope">
<div><p class="small">Our sample</p><div class="sample-preps"><div class="prep">P1</div><div class="prep">P2</div><div class="prep">P3</div><div class="prep">P4</div><div class="prep">P5</div><div class="prep">P6</div></div></div>
<div class="population"><p class="medium">Further preparations<br>of cell line L1</p><p class="small">Under the culture and assay<br>conditions we have specified</p></div>
</div>
<p class="takeaway keyline">The population: preparations we have not made yet. The purpose: predict what the same experiment would show again.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 00:56–01:00 (4 minutes).**

**Say:** Resolve the vote. The six preparations are our sample. The defensible population is option A: further preparations of L1, made under the culture and assay conditions we specified. A population need not be people — here it is the set of experiments we could still run. Land the purpose in one sentence: statistical inference tells us what another six preparations would plausibly show; it does not generalise to other cell lines or patients. Every number in the second half — mean, interval, p-value — answers that question. Options B and C need different experiments, not a better analysis.

**Conceptual point:** In laboratory biology, a population is defined by the scope of the intended inference and the process that could generate new experimental units.

**Likely misconception:** Repeating a single cell line samples the population of all human cells, or the population is automatically everything in the incubator.

**Optional follow-up:** Would a new serum lot still fall inside your intended claim?

**Sources:** R pp. 16–33, especially 30–33; A pp. 56–58, 63, 71; D pp. 9–20. Rebuilt sampling-space idea with the recurring assay rather than M&Ms or BMI data.
:::
